title: One order.
One safe retry.
payment.intro: Follow a payment when the response is lost. See how one key prevents a second charge.

steps.title: Start with the request.
steps.body: The customer places an order. The request includes a stable ID. A retry will use the same ID.
steps.label: The customer sends an order.
steps.note: The request includes a stable request ID.

steps.title: Save before you charge.
steps.body: The API creates a pending operation. It stores a payment key with the request ID. The store enforces a unique request ID for each customer.
steps.label: The API stores the operation.
steps.note: The request ID and payment key are saved together.

steps.title: Charge with the saved key.
steps.body: The API sends the payment key to the payment service. The service uses this key to identify the operation.
steps.label: The API sends the payment key.
steps.note: The payment service uses the key to identify the charge.

steps.title: The response is lost.
steps.body: The charge succeeds. The API stops before it saves the result. The stored operation still says “pending.”
steps.label: The charge succeeds. The API stops.
steps.note: The result is lost. The saved operation remains pending.

steps.title: Find the first operation.
steps.body: The customer retries with the same request ID. The API reads the pending operation and gets its original payment key.
steps.label: The customer retries.
steps.note: The API reads the original payment key.

steps.title: Recover the result.
steps.body: The API retries with the same payment key. Under the service’s idempotency rules, it gets the existing result. It saves the result and confirms the order.
steps.caveat: If the key has expired, the API must reconcile the charge before it starts a new operation.
steps.label: The API recovers the result.
steps.note: The same key returns the existing payment result.

title: One product.
One faster read.
cache.intro: Follow a cache miss, then a cache hit. See where fresh data still matters.

steps.title: Ask for a product.
steps.body: The customer opens a product page. The API receives an item ID and asks the cache for the item.
steps.label: The customer requests an item.
steps.note: The API uses the item ID as the cache key.

steps.title: Check the cache.
steps.body: The key is absent. The cache cannot answer this request, so the API must read the source data.
steps.label: The cache reports a miss.
steps.note: A miss sends this request to the database.

steps.title: Read the source.
steps.body: The API reads the product from the database. The database remains the source of truth.
steps.label: The API reads the database.
steps.note: The response contains the current stored product.

steps.title: Save a short copy.
steps.body: The API places the product in the cache with an expiry time. It then returns the product to the customer.
steps.label: The API fills the cache.
steps.note: The copy has a defined lifetime.

steps.title: Serve the next read.
steps.body: The next request finds the item in the cache. The API can answer without a database read.
steps.label: The cache returns the product.
steps.note: The faster path can return data that is briefly stale.

steps.title: Check critical values again.
steps.body: When the customer places an order, the order path checks price and stock against authoritative data. A page-view cache is not enough for this decision.
steps.label: The order path checks the source.
steps.note: Do not use a stale page copy to confirm stock or price.

title: One job.
One safe redelivery.
queue.intro: Follow a queued task when a worker stops. See why delivery and completion are separate.

steps.title: Accept the job.
steps.body: The client submits work that can finish after the request ends. The API assigns a stable job ID.
steps.label: The client submits a job.
steps.note: A stable ID helps detect repeated work.

steps.title: Save the message.
steps.body: The API writes a message to the queue. It confirms acceptance only after the queue accepts the message.
steps.label: The API sends the job to the queue.
steps.note: The message carries the job ID and required input.

steps.title: Give work to a worker.
steps.body: A worker receives the message. The queue keeps it available for redelivery until it is acknowledged.
steps.label: The worker receives the job.
steps.note: Receipt is not proof that the job finished.

steps.title: The worker stops.
steps.body: The worker stops before it acknowledges the message. The queue makes the message available again after its visibility period.
steps.label: The worker fails before acknowledgement.
steps.note: The message can be delivered again.

steps.title: Run the job again.
steps.body: Another worker receives the same job ID. It checks completed work before repeating an external effect.
steps.label: A second worker checks the job ID.
steps.note: Consumers must tolerate duplicate delivery.

steps.title: Mark completion.
steps.body: After the effect and its result are recorded, the worker acknowledges the message. A failed job can move to a dead-letter queue after a defined retry limit.
steps.label: The worker acknowledges the job.
steps.note: A retry limit keeps poison messages from looping forever.

title: One request.
One fair limit.
rate.intro: Follow a request through a rate limiter. See what changes when the counter store fails.

steps.title: Identify the caller.
steps.body: The client sends a request. The gateway selects a limit key such as an authenticated account ID.
steps.label: The gateway identifies the caller.
steps.note: The key controls which requests share a limit.

steps.title: Check the current window.
steps.body: The gateway checks the caller’s count in the counter store. It uses an atomic operation so concurrent requests do not all pass the same limit.
steps.label: The gateway checks the count.
steps.note: The check and update must be atomic.

steps.title: Forward allowed work.
steps.body: If the count is below the limit, the gateway updates it and forwards the request to the service.
steps.label: The gateway allows the request.
steps.note: The service receives only permitted work.

steps.title: Stop excess work.
steps.body: When the caller reaches the limit, the gateway returns a rate-limit response and a retry hint. It does not forward the request.
steps.label: The gateway rejects excess work.
steps.note: The client can wait before it retries.

steps.title: Define a failure rule.
steps.body: If the counter store is unavailable, the gateway follows a documented fail-open or fail-closed rule for this endpoint.
steps.label: The counter store is unavailable.
steps.note: The fallback depends on the cost and risk of this endpoint.

steps.title: Resume normal checks.
steps.body: When the store returns, the gateway resumes atomic checks. It monitors rejected requests and store errors to detect an unsafe limit.
steps.label: The gateway resumes checks.
steps.note: Monitor both rejection rate and counter-store health.
